design_detail: ADAPT-2: multisite, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial using a two-stage sequential parallel comparison design, run at eight US sites from 23 May 2017 to 25 July 2019 in the NIDA Clinical Trials Network. Adults with moderate or severe DSM-5 methamphetamine-type stimulant use disorder were randomized 0.26:0.74 to extended-release injectable naltrexone (380 mg every 3 weeks) plus oral extended-release bupropion (450 mg daily) or to matching injectable and oral placebo for 6 weeks (stage 1); people in the placebo group without a response were re-randomized 1:1 to the same comparison for a further 6 weeks (stage 2). The primary outcome combined the two stages with weights of 0.43 and 0.57.
can_establish: Whether, over 6 to 12 weeks in treatment-seeking adults with moderate or severe methamphetamine use disorder, this drug combination produced more people meeting a urine-defined response than placebo, and the size of that difference in percentage points.
cannot_establish: Whether the benefit persists after the 12-week medication period (no post-treatment follow-up outcome is reported here); which of the two drugs, or their combination, is responsible (no single-agent arms); effects on use outside the two-week evaluation windows, on functioning or on mortality; effectiveness outside a trial with twice-weekly visits, weekly clinician contact, adherence technology and payment; or the separate contribution of each component to adverse events.

sample.recruitment: Community advertising (print, web, radio, television) and direct referral (from enrolled participants, medical clinics, social-service agencies) near eight US sites: Pickens SC, Portland OR, Minneapolis, New York, San Francisco, Los Angeles and two in Dallas. Participants were paid; amounts are in the protocol, which was not read.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: adults 18 to 65 who wanted to stop or reduce methamphetamine use; DSM-5 moderate or severe stimulant use disorder, methamphetamine type; methamphetamine use on at least 18 of the 30 days before consent; two or more methamphetamine-positive urine samples at least 2 days apart within 10 days before randomization; opioid-free at randomization. Excluded: concurrent treatment for substance use disorder; expected need for opioid-containing medication; conditions raising seizure risk or contraindicated medications. Other medical and psychiatric diagnoses were assessed case by case rather than excluded automatically.
sample.demographics: All randomized participants (n=403): mean age 41.0 years (SD 10.1); 68.7% men; 71.2% White, 11.9% Black, 16.9% other; 13.6% Hispanic or Latino; 38.7% employed; 35.2% with high-school education or less. Methamphetamine use on 26.7 (SD 4.1) of the previous 30 days; most frequent route smoking 72.7%, intravenous 19.1%, nasal or oral 8.2%; 33.5% reported any intravenous use in the previous 30 days; mean age at first use 24.8 years; baseline craving 66.1 of 100; PHQ-9 19.9 (SD 6.5). Co-occurring DSM-5 disorders among those assessed: alcohol 32.1% (94/293), cannabis 36.5% (116/318), cocaine 8.5% (31/365), opioid 7.3% (27/370); daily cigarette smoking 70.6% (238/337); HIV-positive 25.3% (90/356).
sample.attrition: Participants with two or more missing urine results, or who discontinued, were counted as non-responders, so attrition is folded into the primary outcome rather than reported separately in the text; the flow diagram (Figure 1) is an image. The prespecified complete-case analysis shows how many provided all four evaluation-window samples: stage 1, 52 of 109 (47.7%) on naltrexone-bupropion and 177 of 294 (60.2%) on placebo; stage 2, 80 of 114 (70.2%) and 75 of 111 (67.6%). Adherence in stage 1 was 75.1% on naltrexone-bupropion (oral 63.9%, injection 86.2%) and 83.5% on placebo (74.1%, 92.7%); in stage 2, 77.4% (68.8%, 86.4%) and 82.0% (75.1%, 89.2%).
sample.selection_effects: Treatment-seeking volunteers who wanted to reduce or stop use, were able to attend twice-weekly visits for 12 weeks, were opioid-free at entry and were using almost daily (mean 27 of 30 days). People in opioid treatment or needing opioid analgesia were excluded, which matters given the overlap of methamphetamine and opioid use. Women were 31% of the sample. The discussion notes that the low attrition and high adherence achieved in the trial may themselves limit generalizability to routine practice.

exposure.measurement: Assigned study medication, not drug use: extended-release injectable naltrexone 380 mg or matching placebo injection given by trial clinicians on the randomization day and in week 3 of each stage, plus oral extended-release bupropion titrated over 3 days to 450 mg daily (reducible to 300 mg for adverse effects, with encouragement to return to target) or matching placebo, tapered over 4 days at week 13. Oral adherence was by self-report with tablet counts and a smartphone application; injection adherence was documented by staff.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as above, for 6 weeks per stage and up to 12 weeks in total. Participants' methamphetamine use at entry: a mean of 26.7 of the previous 30 days, mostly smoked.
exposure.polysubstance: Co-occurring alcohol, cannabis, cocaine and opioid use disorders were present (see demographics) and were not exclusion criteria, except that people were required to be opioid-free at randomization and not in concurrent substance-use treatment. Urine was tested for 10 drugs but only methamphetamine results are reported in the paper; other-substance outcomes are registered but not reported here.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: the outcome is methamphetamine-negative urine during the trial. Samples were validated by temperature strip (32 to 38 degrees C) and an adulterant test and read on point-of-care cards; twice-weekly collection gave up to 12 samples per stage.

comparison.controls: Matched injectable and oral placebo, given on the same schedule by the same clinicians.
comparison.matching: Randomization in a 0.26:0.74 ratio in stage 1 and 1:1 at re-randomization; the method of sequence generation and allocation concealment is not described in the paper (it is in the protocol, not read). Baseline characteristics are tabulated by arm and stage.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison. Chance imbalances at re-randomization are visible in Table 1: in stage 2, the naltrexone-bupropion arm had fewer Black participants (7.0% vs 19.8%), more White participants (73.7% vs 62.2%) and more daily cigarette smokers (82.0% vs 62.9%) than the placebo arm; in stage 1 the Treatment Effectiveness Assessment score was 16.7 vs 18.6.

outcomes.instruments: Primary: response, defined as at least three of four possible methamphetamine-negative urine samples in the last 2 weeks of a stage (weeks 5 to 6, or weeks 11 to 12), counted in the stage where it first occurred, with two or more missing samples or discontinuation counted as non-response. Secondary: percentage of methamphetamine-negative urine samples (negatives divided by the 12 expected per stage); worst methamphetamine craving in the past week on a 0 to 100 visual analogue scale; PHQ-9 depressive symptoms (0 to 27); Treatment Effectiveness Assessment, a participant-reported 4-item scale (4 to 40). Safety: participant-reported adverse events coded to MedDRA 22.1, vital signs, liver-function tests, injection-site reactions, electrocardiograms and suicidality, with serious events adjudicated by a sponsor-appointed medical monitor.
outcomes.validity_norms: Urine drug screening is an objective outcome and the response definition is stringent (at least 3 of 4 negatives in a 2-week window). The chosen window captures use only in the final 2 weeks of each stage; the registered secondary measures covering the earlier weeks are not reported in this paper. The Treatment Effectiveness Assessment used here (self-report) is not the same measure as the urine-based 'Treatment Effectiveness Score' registered as a secondary outcome.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Response' is abstinence-like behaviour in a 2-week window, not remission, functioning or sustained abstinence. The overall treatment effect is the difference between groups in the weighted average response across stages (weights 0.43 and 0.57).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None for the four secondary outcomes: the paper states that no multiplicity adjustment was prespecified and that no clinical conclusions can be drawn from them. The primary outcome was tested once, one-sided at alpha 0.025. Adverse events were compared with Fisher's exact tests across dozens of event terms with no adjustment.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Participants, trial clinicians and site investigators were reported as unaware of assignment (registry lists quadruple masking); the primary outcome is a laboratory urine result, so assessor judgment plays little part. Blinding integrity was not assessed, and the adverse-event profile (nausea 37.6% vs 15.3% in stage 1) makes functional unblinding plausible.

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary (intention-to-treat): stage 1, 18 of 109 (16.5%) responded on naltrexone-bupropion versus 10 of 294 (3.4%) on placebo; stage 2, 13 of 114 (11.4%) versus 2 of 111 (1.8%). Weighted response 13.6% versus 2.5%; treatment effect 11.1 percentage points (SE 2.5; one-sided 95% lower boundary 6.3; Wald z=4.53; P<0.001); number needed to treat 9. Editors' calculations of the stage-specific absolute effects: stage 1 risk difference 13.1 percentage points (95% CI 5.8 to 20.4), risk ratio 4.86 (2.31 to 10.19), NNT 8; stage 2 risk difference 9.6 percentage points (95% CI 3.3 to 15.9), risk ratio 6.33 (1.46 to 27.41), NNT 10; two-sided 95% interval for the weighted effect, from the reported SE, 6.2 to 16.0 percentage points. Prespecified sensitivity analyses: complete cases (all four samples provided) gave 15 of 52 (28.8%) versus 9 of 177 (5.1%) in stage 1 and 13 of 80 (16.2%) versus 1 of 75 (1.3%) in stage 2, overall effect 18.7 percentage points (95% CI 11.6 to 25.8); equal stage weights gave 11.4 percentage points (95% CI 6.5 to 16.2). Secondary outcomes (weighted differences, SE): methamphetamine-negative urine samples 6.8 percentage points (95% CI 3.5 to 10.1); craving -9.7 points (-13.8 to -5.6); PHQ-9 -1.1 points (-1.9 to -0.2); Treatment Effectiveness Assessment +4.0 points (2.3 to 5.7).
analysis.covariates: None in the primary analysis. Prespecified subgroup effects by site, sex, race, ethnic group and age were estimated with generalized linear mixed models and shown in a supplementary forest plot (not read).
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03078075, first submitted 2 March 2017 and first posted 13 March 2017, before the first enrolment on 23 May 2017; results first posted 29 March 2021. The registry lists two separate primary outcome measures, the number of participants with a treatment response at the end of stage 1 (week 6) and at the end of stage 2 (week 12), with the same at-least-3-of-4 definition; the paper's primary outcome is the weighted combination of the two stages, which is specified in the statistical analysis plan inside the protocol rather than in the registry. The paper reports the stage-specific counts as well, so both forms are available. Registered secondary outcomes include a urine-based 'Treatment Effectiveness Score', maximum consecutive negative screens, weeks with two negative screens, self-reported abstinent days (timeline followback), craving and PHQ-9; the paper reports craving, PHQ-9, percentage of negative samples and a self-reported Treatment Effectiveness Assessment, so several registered secondary outcomes are not in this article. The sample size was increased from 370 to 400 after a prespecified blinded reestimation on the first 185 participants.
analysis.selective_reporting: Several registered secondary outcomes (self-reported abstinent days, consecutive negative screens, other-substance outcomes) are absent from the paper. Adverse events are tabulated only for events of interest occurring in at least 3% of the naltrexone-bupropion group or with P at most 0.05, with the full list in an unread supplement. Post-treatment follow-up visits at weeks 13 and 16 are mentioned in a figure legend but no outcome after week 12 is reported.
analysis.power: Planned at 90% power for 370 participants under assumed response rates of 24% versus 15% (stage 1) and 24% versus 10% (stage 2); the data and safety monitoring board raised the target to 400 after reestimation. Actual responses were much lower in both arms than assumed (16.5% and 3.4%), so the trial was powered for a different scenario than the one observed; it nonetheless reached significance because the placebo response was far lower than assumed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Over 6 weeks per stage, a response (at least 3 of 4 negative urine samples in the final fortnight) occurred in 16.5% on naltrexone-bupropion versus 3.4% on placebo in stage 1 and 11.4% versus 1.8% in stage 2, a weighted difference of 11.1 percentage points (number needed to treat 9). Most participants in both groups did not respond. The average percentage of methamphetamine-negative samples rose by about 7 percentage points, from roughly 12 to 13% on placebo to roughly 19 to 20% on active treatment, so most urine samples were still positive in the treated group. Adverse events were more frequent on active treatment, mainly gastrointestinal and autonomic.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and the final sentence state that the response over 12 weeks was low but higher than with placebo, which matches the data. The claims that sit ahead of the evidence are smaller and mostly in the discussion: the trial's strengths are given as "low attrition, high adherence", while under half of the naltrexone-bupropion group in stage 1 provided all four evaluation samples and oral adherence in that group was 63.9%; the secondary outcomes are said to point in the same direction while the paper itself says no conclusions can be drawn from them; and the abstract reports that serious adverse events occurred in 8 of 223 participants (3.6%) receiving naltrexone-bupropion, whereas the results and Table 3 describe 8 serious adverse events in that group, in fewer participants. Nothing in the paper claims durable abstinence or recovery, and the authors explicitly call for replication in a more naturalistic design.

timeline.event: Elkashef et al.: bupropion alone for methamphetamine dependence, limited efficacy (cited in the introduction).
Heinzerling et al. and later Anderson et al. (2015): bupropion trials in people with less-than-daily use (cited in the introduction).
Open-label pilot of naltrexone plus bupropion suggesting benefit in severe methamphetamine use disorder, the basis for the assumed 24% response rate (cited as reference 19).
ADAPT-2: this trial, 403 participants, weighted treatment effect 11.1 percentage points.

replication.where_it_stands: A single, well-conducted multisite trial with a complex design and a modest absolute effect. Replication in a conventional parallel-group design, with single-agent arms and post-treatment follow-up, has not been identified in this reading; the authors themselves call for replication in a more naturalistic effectiveness design.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse of the NIH (awards UG1DA020024, UG1DA013035, UG1DA040316, UG1DA013727, UG1DA015815) and the Department of Health and Human Services (contracts HHSN271201500065C for the clinical coordinating centre and HHSN271201400028C for the data and statistics centre, both to the Emmes Company). Alkermes donated Vivitrol (extended-release injectable naltrexone) and matched placebo under a written agreement with NIDA; AiCure provided the adherence application under a paid subcontract. The paper states neither company had a role in data collection, analysis or writing, and that there were no confidentiality agreements between investigators and the companies.
funding.declared_conflicts: Extensive individual disclosures. The first author reports consulting fees from a long list of pharmaceutical companies including Alkermes, and institutional grant support from Janssen, Johnson & Johnson and PCORI; a second author reports donated drug from Alkermes; one author reports consulting fees from Indivior; one owns stock in CRISPR Therapeutics and Vertex; one reports consulting fees from COMPASS Pathways, Janssen Global Services and others, including the Emmes Company (the trial's coordinating centre); one reports institutional grant support from Brainsway and Reckitt Benckiser, donated drug from Pear Therapeutics and service on Alkermes advisory boards.
funding.affiliations_note: Two authors are NIDA Clinical Trials Network staff (the sponsor) and are listed as authors; data analysis was performed by three authors, two of them from the Emmes Company (the contracted data and statistics centre). The manufacturer of the injectable naltrexone donated the drug and the matching placebo. Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount the result.

what_would_settle_it: A conventional parallel-group trial with naltrexone alone, bupropion alone, the combination and placebo, powered for the observed response rates, with observed or biologically verified oral adherence, a blinding-integrity check, outcomes covering the whole treatment period rather than a 2-week window, and follow-up for at least 6 months after medication stops, reporting absolute abstinence and functional outcomes.

domains.note: Randomization ratios are stated and baseline characteristics are tabulated, but the paper does not describe sequence generation or allocation concealment (these are in the unread protocol). Stage 2 arms differ noticeably in race composition and smoking, consistent with chance in a sample of 225 but unadjusted.

Double-blind with matched injection and tablets and an intention-to-treat analysis, but blinding integrity was not assessed and the active combination produced distinctive adverse effects; oral adherence was self-reported and lower on active treatment (63.9% vs 74.1% in stage 1), and dose reduction to 300 mg was permitted without the number of reductions being reported.

Handled conservatively: two or more missing samples or discontinuation counted as non-response, which biases towards the null. But missingness was substantial and differential (all four evaluation samples provided by 47.7% of the naltrexone-bupropion group and 60.2% of the placebo group in stage 1), and the complete-case analysis gives a much larger effect (18.7 vs 11.1 percentage points), so the true effect depends on why samples were missing.
Objective urine drug screening with temperature and adulterant checks, twice weekly, with a prespecified response definition applied identically in both arms.

Registered before enrolment, with a statistical analysis plan in the protocol and both prespecified sensitivity analyses reported. However, the registry's primary outcomes are the two stage-specific response counts while the paper's headline is the weighted combination; several registered secondary outcomes are not reported; adverse events are tabulated selectively in the main paper; and an interim efficacy analysis was performed by the data and safety monitoring board with no adjustment of the significance level, which the authors acknowledge.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The result is based on a registered, multisite, double-blind trial with an objective outcome and a conservative handling of missing data, and the direction and significance of the effect are unlikely to be artefacts. Concerns that keep it from low risk: undescribed allocation concealment, unverified blinding with a drug combination that produces recognizable effects, substantial and differential missing urine samples whose treatment changes the estimate by a factor of nearly two, an unadjusted interim efficacy look, and a headline outcome in a weighted form that differs from the registry's stage-specific primary outcomes. None of these would plausibly manufacture the 11.1-percentage-point difference, but they affect its size.

key_findings.finding: 403 adults with moderate or severe DSM-5 methamphetamine-type stimulant use disorder were randomized in stage 1 (109 to naltrexone-bupropion, 294 to placebo) and 225 placebo non-responders were re-randomized in stage 2 (114 and 111) at eight US sites between 23 May 2017 and 25 July 2019.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Trial design and conduct; Results › Participants, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Primary outcome, stage 1: a response (at least 3 of 4 methamphetamine-negative urine samples in weeks 5 to 6) occurred in 18 of 109 (16.5%) on naltrexone-bupropion and 10 of 294 (3.4%) on placebo. Editors' calculation: risk difference 13.1 percentage points (95% CI 5.8 to 20.4), risk ratio 4.86 (2.31 to 10.19).

Primary outcome, stage 2: a response in weeks 11 to 12 occurred in 13 of 114 (11.4%) on naltrexone-bupropion and 2 of 111 (1.8%) on placebo. Editors' calculation: risk difference 9.6 percentage points (95% CI 3.3 to 15.9), risk ratio 6.33 (1.46 to 27.41).

Weighted across stages (weights 0.43 for stage 1 and 0.57 for stage 2), the response was 13.6% on naltrexone-bupropion and 2.5% on placebo: a treatment effect of 11.1 percentage points (SE 2.5; one-sided 95% lower boundary 6.3; Wald z=4.53; P<0.001). The paper gives the number needed to treat as 9. Editors' calculation from the reported SE: two-sided 95% interval 6.2 to 16.0 percentage points.
key_findings.locator: Results › Primary outcome, last sentence; Table 2; Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Prespecified complete-case sensitivity analysis (participants providing all four evaluation samples): stage 1, 15 of 52 (28.8%) versus 9 of 177 (5.1%); stage 2, 13 of 80 (16.2%) versus 1 of 75 (1.3%); overall effect 18.7 percentage points (95% CI 11.6 to 25.8). The denominators imply that only 47.7% of the stage 1 naltrexone-bupropion group and 60.2% of the stage 1 placebo group provided all four samples.
key_findings.note: The complete-case effect is about 69% larger than the intention-to-treat effect, so the conclusion's magnitude depends on how missing samples are treated.

key_findings.finding: Prespecified equal-weight sensitivity analysis gave a treatment effect of 11.4 percentage points (95% CI 6.5 to 16.2), close to the weighted primary analysis.

Secondary outcomes (weighted between-group differences, SE; confidence intervals unadjusted for multiplicity, and the authors state no clinical conclusions can be drawn): methamphetamine-negative urine samples +6.8 percentage points (3.5 to 10.1), from 12.3% and 13.4% on placebo to 20.4% and 19.2% on active treatment in stages 1 and 2; craving on a 0 to 100 scale -9.7 points (-13.8 to -5.6); PHQ-9 -1.1 points (-1.9 to -0.2); Treatment Effectiveness Assessment +4.0 points (2.3 to 5.7).

Adherence: stage 1, 75.1% on naltrexone-bupropion (oral 63.9%, injection 86.2%) versus 83.5% on placebo (74.1%, 92.7%); stage 2, 77.4% (68.8%, 86.4%) versus 82.0% (75.1%, 89.2%). Oral adherence was participant-reported with tablet counts; ingestion was not observed.

Adverse events more frequent on naltrexone-bupropion than placebo (P<0.05): nausea 37.6% vs 15.3% (stage 1) and 28.1% vs 7.2% (stage 2); vomiting 11.9% vs 2.0% and 10.5% vs 2.7%; and, in stage 1, constipation 9.2% vs 2.4%, dry mouth 8.3% vs 1.7%, upper abdominal pain 4.6% vs 0.3%, dizziness 10.1% vs 2.7%, tremor 4.6% vs 0.3%, feeling jittery 3.7% vs 0.7%, malaise 3.7% vs 0.3%, hyperhidrosis 7.3% vs 1.0%, decreased appetite 7.3% vs 2.0%. Headache was more frequent on placebo in stage 1 (23.1% vs 11.9%, P=0.01).

Serious adverse events: 17 in total across the trial, 8 in the naltrexone-bupropion group and 9 in the placebo group; 13 occurred in the intention-to-treat population (stage 1: 1 participant (0.9%) on active treatment and 4 (1.4%) on placebo; stage 2: 3 (2.6%) and 4 (3.6%)). Named events on naltrexone-bupropion were gastroenteritis, homicidal ideation, cellulitis, neck pain and hyperglycaemia; on placebo, substance-induced psychosis, paranoia, pancreatitis, seizure, shigella gastroenteritis, pneumonia, urosepsis and being the victim of a crime.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety, 1st paragraph; Table 3 and its footnotes
key_findings.note: The abstract describes this as serious adverse events in 8 of 223 participants (3.6%) receiving naltrexone-bupropion; Table 3 counts 4 such participants in the intention-to-treat population, so the abstract appears to count events as participants.

key_findings.finding: Baseline severity: participants used methamphetamine on a mean of 26.7 of the 30 days before consent, mostly by smoking (72.7%); 33.5% reported intravenous use in that period; mean PHQ-9 was 19.9 (a severe range); 25.3% of those tested were HIV-positive.

The sample size was increased from 370 to 400 after a prespecified reestimation on the first 185 participants; the data and safety monitoring board, which also reviewed an interim efficacy analysis, recommended the increase, and no adjustment was made to the significance level of the primary test.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03078075, first posted 13 March 2017 (before the first enrolment on 23 May 2017), with results posted 29 March 2021. The registry's primary outcome measures are the two stage-specific response counts at weeks 6 and 12; the article's primary outcome is their weighted combination, prespecified in the statistical analysis plan within the protocol.
key_findings.locator: Primary Outcome Measures; Study Record Dates
key_findings.note: Read from the registry page, not from the article; the article reports both the stage-specific counts and the weighted combination.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that serious adverse events occurred in 8 of 223 participants (3.6%) who received naltrexone-bupropion, while the results section describes 8 serious adverse events in that group and Table 3 reports 1 participant in stage 1 and 3 in stage 2 with at least one such event (plus 3 events among participants who were not re-randomized).
reporting_issues.consequence: Events are presented as participants; the participant-level rate of serious adverse events on active treatment is lower than the abstract implies, and the two groups had similar numbers (8 versus 9 events).

reporting_issues.issue: The footnote to Table 3 states that of 17 serious adverse events in the safety population, 13 occurred in the intention-to-treat population, then lists 4 further events that occurred after consent but before randomization and 4 more in stage 2 participants who were not re-randomized, which totals 21.
reporting_issues.consequence: The serious-adverse-event accounting cannot be reconciled exactly; the main text's split (13 in the intention-to-treat population plus 4 in non-re-randomized participants equals 17) is internally consistent, so the four pre-randomization events appear to be additional and outside the 17.

reporting_issues.issue: The safety population is defined in Table 3's first footnote as all participants who underwent randomization and in the second footnote as all participants who gave informed consent.
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominator for adverse-event rates is ambiguous, which also affects the 8-of-223 figure in the abstract.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion lists low attrition and high adherence among the trial's strengths, while the complete-case analysis shows that fewer than half of the stage 1 naltrexone-bupropion group provided all four evaluation-window urine samples and oral adherence in that group was 63.9%.
reporting_issues.consequence: The characterization of attrition and adherence is more favourable than the reported figures; the discussion then uses low attrition and high adherence as a reason that results may not generalize to practice, which compounds the tension.

reporting_issues.issue: The flow diagram (Figure 1) and the subgroup forest plot (Figure S2) are images, and no numeric breakdown of discontinuation by arm appears in the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Attrition by arm and stage, and subgroup effects by sex, race, age and site, cannot be extracted from the article text; the supplement would be needed.

reporting_issues.issue: The confidence interval for the primary outcome is given only as a one-sided lower boundary of 6.3 percentage points, while the sensitivity analyses are reported with two-sided intervals.
reporting_issues.consequence: The primary estimate's upper bound is not printed; from the reported standard error of 2.5 the two-sided 95% interval is about 6.2 to 16.0 percentage points (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: The trial's registered secondary outcome 'Treatment Effectiveness Score' is a urine-based measure, while the paper's secondary outcome 'Treatment Effectiveness Assessment' is a participant-reported 4-item scale; several other registered secondary outcomes (self-reported abstinent days, maximum consecutive negative screens, weeks with two negative screens, other-substance outcomes) are not reported in the article.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers matching the paper against the registry may conflate two different measures with similar names, and the article is a partial report of the registered outcome set.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper reports outcomes only to week 12, although the figure legend mentions visits at weeks 13 and 16.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether any difference persisted after medication stopped cannot be judged from this article.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC8111570 (author manuscript; all sections, Tables 1, 2 and 3 with footnotes rendered as text, acknowledgements, funding and disclosures read; Figures 1 and 2 are images and their values were not extracted; the protocol, statistical analysis plan and supplementary appendix were not read). Registration details additionally read from the ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT03078075.
